section.title: Israel's Only Savior
section.sectionRationale: Continuing the Book of Comfort, this chapter presses the polemic against idols into its most personal form yet: the LORD who formed Israel and calls it by name declares Himself the only Savior there has ever been or ever will be, promising a new exodus through the waters and the desert, even as He honestly names Israel's failure to call on Him at all.
section.thesis: The LORD who formed and redeemed Israel declares Himself its one and only Savior, before whom no god was formed and after whom none will come, and promises a new way through the wilderness even for a people who, by their own admission, grew weary of Him and did not call upon His name.
section.frameNote: Seven movements: do not fear, for I have redeemed you; the promised gathering of exiles from every direction; the courtroom declaration that the LORD alone is God and Savior; a further word of coming rescue from Babylon; the announcement of a new thing, a way in the wilderness; Israel's failure to call on the LORD in worship; and the closing promise that the LORD blots out transgressions for His own sake.

units.label: Do not fear, I have redeemed you

verses.text: Now this is what the LORD says, He who {{bara|created}} you, O Jacob, and He who formed you, O Israel: “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine!

When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched; the flames will not set you ablaze.
For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior; I give Egypt for your ransom, Cush and Seba in your place.
Because you are precious and honored in My sight, and because I love you, I will give men in exchange for you and nations in place of your life.

units.label: I will bring your offspring from every direction

verses.text: Do not be afraid, for I am with you; I will bring your offspring from the east and gather you from the west.
I will say to the north, ‘Give them up!’ and to the south, ‘Do not hold them back!’ Bring My sons from afar, and My daughters from the ends of the earth,
everyone called by My name and created for My glory, whom I have indeed formed and made.”
Bring out a people who have eyes but are blind, and who have ears but are deaf.

All the nations gather together and the peoples assemble. Who among them can declare this, and proclaim to us the former things? Let them present their witnesses to vindicate them, so that others may hear and say, “It is true.”

“You are My witnesses,” declares the LORD, “and My servant whom I have chosen, so that you may consider and believe Me and understand that I am He. Before Me no god was formed, and after Me none will come.
I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me.
I alone decreed and saved and proclaimed, I, and not some foreign god among you. So you are My witnesses,” declares the LORD, “that I am God.
Even from eternity I am He, and none can deliver out of My hand. When I act, who can reverse it?”
Thus says the LORD your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: “For your sake, I will send to Babylon and bring them all as fugitives, even the Chaldeans, in the ships in which they rejoice.
I am the LORD, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, and your King.”

units.label: Behold, I am about to do something new

verses.text: Thus says the LORD, who makes a way in the sea and a path through the surging waters,
who brings out the chariots and horses, the armies and warriors together, to lie down, never to rise again; to be extinguished, snuffed out like a wick:
“Do not call to mind the former things; pay no attention to the things of old.
Behold, I am about to do something new; even now it is coming. Do you not see it? Indeed, I will make a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert.
The beasts of the field will honor Me, the jackals and the ostriches, because I provide water in the wilderness and rivers in the desert, to give drink to My chosen people.
The people I formed for Myself will declare My praise.

units.label: You have not called on Me

verses.text: But you have not called on Me, O Jacob, because you have grown weary of Me, O Israel.
You have not brought Me sheep for burnt offerings, nor honored Me with your sacrifices. I have not burdened you with offerings, nor wearied you with frankincense.
You have not bought Me sweet cane with your silver, nor satisfied Me with the fat of your sacrifices. But you have burdened Me with your sins; you have wearied Me with your iniquities.
I, yes I, am He who {{machah|blots out}} your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more.
Remind Me, let us argue the matter together. State your case, so that you may be vindicated.
Your first father sinned, and your spokesmen rebelled against Me.
So I will disgrace the princes of your sanctuary, and I will devote Jacob to destruction and Israel to reproach.”

bara.gloss: To create, a verb Scripture reserves exclusively for God's own creative act, used first of the heavens and the earth in Genesis 1:1. Here it is applied personally to Israel, the same God who created the cosmos also created this particular people for Himself, grounding their identity and security in His creative, not merely their own historical, origin.

machah.gloss: To blot out, wipe away, erase completely, as one wipes a slate clean or a name from a record. The LORD declares He blots out Israel's transgressions for His own sake, not because they earned it, and the same word pictures total, irreversible removal, not partial or temporary forgiveness, a promise the New Testament shows fulfilled completely in Christ.

basic.context: This chapter moves from tender reassurance, do not fear, I have redeemed you, to a courtroom scene where the LORD alone stands as God and Savior, to the electrifying announcement of a new exodus through the wilderness, and finally to an honest and painful diagnosis: Israel had grown weary of God and stopped calling on Him, yet He still promises to blot out their sin for His own sake.
basic.hermeneutics: The immediate promise addresses exiles who will be gathered from Babylon and beyond, a real historical return under Cyrus. But its language of passing through waters and fire, and making a way in the wilderness, deliberately echoes the exodus from Egypt, presenting the return from exile as a new exodus, a pattern of redemption that reaches its fullest sense in Christ's own greater deliverance from sin and death.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel is the people the LORD Himself {{bara}}, created, and formed, not a nation that made itself, and this same LORD promises to {{machah}}, blot out, its transgressions completely, for His own sake rather than because of anything Israel has done to deserve it. Both words underline that Israel's whole existence, from creation to forgiveness, rests entirely on God's initiative.
basic.typology: The new way through the wilderness, streams in the desert, and a path through the sea, verses 16 to 20, deliberately echoes the exodus from Egypt and anticipates the greater new exodus Christ accomplishes, His own decisive act of deliverance that Luke 9:31 actually calls His 'exodus,' accomplished at Jerusalem. The declaration that there is no Savior but the LORD, verse 11, anticipates the New Testament's insistence that salvation is found in no one but Jesus, Acts 4:12.
basic.christ: The LORD's declaration, 'I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me,' verse 11, is fulfilled in Jesus, of whom Peter says, 'there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved,' Acts 4:12. The promise that God 'blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more,' verse 25, is the same complete forgiveness secured at the cross, since only God can forgive sins, Mark 2:7, and Jesus does exactly that.
basic.god: God is Israel's Creator, Redeemer, and only Savior, before whom no rival god was ever formed and after whom none will come. He is honest about His people's weariness and failure to call on Him, yet He forgives not because they earned it but for His own name's sake, blotting out transgressions completely and remembering them no more.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 4:12 declares salvation is found in no name but Jesus, echoing the LORD's exclusive claim in verse 11. Mark 2:7-10 shows Jesus forgiving sins, an authority the Pharisees rightly recognize belongs to God alone. Luke 9:31 calls Christ's coming death His 'exodus,' fulfilling the new exodus imagery of this chapter. 1 Corinthians 10:1-4 treats the first exodus as a type pointing forward to Christ.
basic.oneStory: This chapter's movement from redemption, through a courtroom declaring the LORD the only Savior, to a new exodus, and finally to grace despite Israel's weariness, traces the whole Bible's pattern of God's initiative in saving a people who cannot save themselves. It anticipates Christ, the only Savior, whose own exodus at the cross accomplishes the final and complete blotting out of sin this chapter promises.

context.literary:
The chapter is stitched from a pattern that Isaiah uses all through this part of the book: a word of salvation, 'Do not fear,' followed by a word of argument. Verses 1 to 7 are the salvation oracle, and its structure is plain. It opens with a messenger formula and a pair of past-tense verbs, 'created' and 'formed,' then the central 'Do not fear,' then a series of 'I will' promises, and it ends where it began, with God's creative work, 'created for My glory,' verse 7. The oracle is bracketed by creation, and the redemption sits in the middle of it.

Verses 8 to 13 turn into a courtroom. A blind and deaf people is summoned in verse 8, the nations are called to assemble in verse 9, and the question is who can declare the former things. Israel is then given a role that sounds surprising, that of witness, and the LORD is both judge and the party whose reputation is at stake. The refrain 'I, yes I' in verse 11, and again in verse 25, marks the two points where God stakes everything on His own character.

Verses 14 to 21 shift to two short messenger formulas, each prefaced by a divine title, and between them a memory and a command to forget. Verses 22 to 28 end with a second trial, this time with Israel as the defendant, 'Remind Me, let us argue the matter together,' verse 26. It is no accident that the chapter begins with 'created you' and finishes with 'devote Jacob to destruction.' The same God who made Israel names what Israel has done with that gift. Grace is placed in the center, verse 25, between two lists of accusations, verses 22 to 24 and 26 to 28.
context.historical:
The geography of verses 3 to 7 is a map of the world as the exiles knew it. Egypt, Cush and Seba are named as the price of Israel's release. Cush lay far up the Nile, and Seba is usually placed in that same southern region, which the BSB footnote on verse 3 calls the upper Nile region. These were wealthy and distant lands, and the claim is that God will pay, as it were, in the world's most valuable currency. The four points of the compass in verses 5 and 6 describe a scattering that began with Assyria's deportations in the eighth century and deepened with Babylon's in the sixth, and so the exiles were not only in Babylon but spread across the east, the north and the south.

The reference to Babylon in verse 14 would have startled hearers. Babylon was then the great power of the age, with a canal-and-river economy that made the 'ships' of verse 14 a point of national pride. The text of that verse is difficult in Hebrew, and translators differ on details of the phrase about the Chaldeans' ships, but its direction is clear: the proud city will be brought down and its people will flee. The conquest by Persia in 539 BC lies at the other end of this promise, though the prophet does not name Cyrus here and keeps him for chapters 44 and 45.

The charge about offerings in verses 22 to 24 has to be read against the exile, when there was no temple in which to offer them. Some readers think the prophet is looking back to the long centuries when the offerings were given with a divided heart, as in Isaiah 1:11-15 and Malachi 1:6-8. Others hold that he is describing the exiles' present neglect of calling on the LORD. In either case the prophet's point is that God never needed their gifts, verse 23, and that the burden in the relationship had run the other way.
context.canonical:
Isaiah 43 draws on the first exodus and on the original covenant promises, and it is drawn on in turn. The water and fire of verse 2 recall both the crossing of the sea, Exodus 14:21-22, and the Jordan, Joshua 3:14-17. The psalmist uses the same pairing, 'we went through fire and water,' Psalm 66:12. The claim that no one saves but the LORD restates older confessions of Israel, Deuteronomy 32:39 and Hosea 13:4.

The 'new thing' of verse 19 anchors a theme in the rest of Isaiah. Chapter 48 says the new things are declared before they spring forth, 48:6-7, chapter 51 calls on the arm of the LORD to do again what He did at the sea, 51:9-10, and chapter 65 announces new heavens and a new earth, 65:17. The New Testament carries this up: Luke names the death of Jesus His 'exodus,' Luke 9:31, Paul says that in Christ there is a new creation, 2 Corinthians 5:17, and the voice from the throne in Revelation 21:5 says, 'Behold, I make all things new.'

The promise to remember sins no more, verse 25, comes back in Jeremiah's new covenant, Jeremiah 31:34, and the writer of Hebrews quotes it twice as the basis for a sacrifice that never has to be repeated, Hebrews 8:12 and 10:17. Peter calls the church 'a people for God's own possession' in the language of verses 20 and 21, 1 Peter 2:9, and in the same breath says they were called out of darkness to declare His praises.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet is answering a fear that sits underneath the whole exile: that Israel's God had been defeated, or that Israel's sin had finally exhausted Him. The opening 'Do not fear' is not a general comfort but a reply to that specific doubt, and its ground is given three times in the opening verses, 'created,' 'redeemed' and 'called by name.' He intends the exiles to hear themselves described by what God has done to them and for them, and not by what they have done.

The courtroom scene gives them a part to play. The nations have their gods but no witnesses who can prove that those gods ever announced anything and then did it. Israel does have such evidence, since the LORD predicted the exile and a return and is now acting on it. The prophet wants a defeated people to understand that they are the key exhibit in the case for who is God.

Then the prophet will not let that comfort slide into complacency. Verses 22 to 24 are written to keep forgiveness from being taken for a right. The surprise is that forgiveness is announced right in the middle of the indictment, verse 25, as though God's grace were something that could not be stopped even by a plain account of the people's failure. The intended response is amazement and a return to calling on Him, not a shrug.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 2 and 3 are promises given to the nation in exile, and they should not be flattened into a guarantee that no believer will ever be hurt by flood or fire. The promise is that God will be with His people in it, and that the waters and flames will not have the last word. The text says 'when,' not 'if,' you pass through, which assumes that suffering is coming. It is a promise of presence and of an end, not a promise of a path with no water.

Similarly, God giving up Egypt, Cush and Seba for Israel's sake is a description of His sovereign dealings with the nations in that historical moment. It does not teach that the nations are cheap, or that God values one people above others in some lasting way. The same book ends with Egypt and Assyria invited into the blessing, Isaiah 19:24-25.

The command in verse 18 'Do not call to mind the former things' has to be read in its setting. It is not a permanent ban on remembering what God has done, since the very prophet has just recalled the exodus in verses 16 and 17 and the Bible tells believers to remember often. It is a call not to let the memory of an earlier rescue become a boundary on what God can do next.

debates.question: Does 'Do not call to mind the former things,' verse 18, forbid remembering the exodus?

views.label: The new eclipses the old
views.case: The new thing is so great that it will make the first exodus fade, as Jeremiah says that people will no longer say 'As the LORD lives who brought Israel out of Egypt,' but 'who brought them out of the north,' Jeremiah 16:14-15. The old rescue is not erased but outshone.

views.label: A call not to be stuck in the past
views.case: The sense is that the exiles should not look back and conclude that God's best work is behind them. The Hebrew is about what they dwell on, not about whether they may recall history. The very next verse says 'Do you not see it?' which is a rebuke to people looking the wrong way.

views.label: The former things are the prophecies already fulfilled
views.case: In verse 9 the same phrase means earlier predictions that came true, and in 42:9 it means things now past. On this view the exiles are told not to rest on those proofs but to expect a new announcement, as Isaiah 42:9 says the LORD declares new things.

debates.bearing: The surrounding verses settle the practical question. The prophet himself has just recalled the sea and the chariots in verses 16 and 17, so he cannot mean that they must be forgotten. The command is a warning against treating a past rescue as a limit on God. Remembering in order to hope is encouraged; remembering in order to despair is not.

debates.question: Is the new exodus only the return from Babylon, or does it reach beyond that?

views.label: The return from Babylon
views.case: Verses 5 to 7 and 14 speak of exiles gathered from the nations and of Babylon's collapse. The decree of Cyrus in Ezra 1 led to a real journey home, and that journey is the plain referent.

views.label: A pattern fulfilled in Christ and the new creation
views.case: The language of a path through the sea, rivers in the desert and gathering from the ends of the earth is larger than the small return from Babylon, which the returnees themselves found disappointing, Haggai 2:3. The New Testament speaks of Christ's death as an exodus, Luke 9:31, and of the gathering of God's scattered children, John 11:52.

debates.bearing: Isaiah gives no sign that he sees these as rivals. The return from Babylon is a first installment of a pattern that the prophets and the Gospels see completed in Christ. A reader should hold the near fulfilment and the far one together, as Peter says the prophets searched carefully to learn the time to which the Spirit pointed, 1 Peter 1:10-11.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verse sets two verbs side by side, yatsar and bara. Bara, create, is used only of God in the Old Testament, and is the verb of Genesis 1:1. Yatsar, form, is the potter's verb, the one used of the man shaped from the dust in Genesis 2:7. Together they say that Israel was both brought into being and carefully shaped by hand. The same verb yatsar appears in verse 10 in a sharp way: 'Before Me no god was formed,' which means that the gods of the nations are the products of a craftsman's hands, a theme taken up in the next chapter.

The word for 'redeemed,' ga'al, belongs to family law. The go'el was a kinsman responsible for buying back land that had been sold, for freeing a relative who had been sold into debt, and for pursuing justice for a murdered relative, Leviticus 25:25 and 25:48-49, and the book of Ruth shows the role at work, Ruth 4:1-6. To say that God is Israel's go'el in verses 1 and 14 is to say that He treats them as His own kin. The perfect tense, 'I have redeemed you,' states the act as already done even though the people are still in Babylon.

The 'ransom,' kofer, in verse 3 is a legal word for the price that spares a life, as in the census money of Exodus 30:12 and the proverb that the wicked become a ransom for the righteous, Proverbs 21:18. When Jesus says He gives His life as a ransom for many, Mark 10:45, He uses a word from that same field of ideas in the Greek of His day.

The phrase 'I am He,' ani hu, appears in verse 10 and again in verse 13, and it is a self-declaration of God that Isaiah uses repeatedly, Isaiah 41:4 and 46:4 among them. The Septuagint renders it 'I am,' ego eimi, and many readers hear an echo of that phrase in the 'I am' sayings of Jesus, such as John 8:24 and 13:19.

The 'witnesses' of verses 10 and 12 are edim, a legal term for those who give testimony in court. Israel's testimony is not a verbal performance but a visible history of announcement and fulfilment.

In verse 24 two verbs sit close together: the LORD says Israel has 'burdened' Him, from the root avad, and 'wearied' Him, from yaga. The root avad is the same one that makes 'servant,' and a reader catches a bitter irony: the servant has made the master serve. Verse 23 says that He had not burdened or wearied them in the same pair of verbs, so the two lines mirror one another.

The 'new thing,' chadashah, 'is about to spring forth,' titsmach, in verse 19, using the verb of a plant that sprouts. The same verb of growth appears in 42:9, 'Before they spring forth,' and again in 44:4 and 45:8, so the prophet lets a single image of green growth carry the idea of the future.

typology.fulfillment: The first exodus passed through the sea and was led by a pillar of fire, Exodus 14:21-22 and 13:21. Paul says the fathers were 'baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,' 1 Corinthians 10:1-2. Isaiah turns that pattern into a promise for every later passage through disaster. In Christ the waters of judgment are crossed in one person: Jesus speaks of His death as a baptism He must undergo, Luke 12:50, and rises through it. The type falls short because Israel passed through water and still perished in the wilderness, 1 Corinthians 10:5, while those united to Christ pass through death into life.

typology.type: The ransom of nations for Israel, verses 3 and 4
typology.fulfillment: God gives Egypt, Cush and Seba in Israel's place, a substitution that pictures the cost of redemption. The nations here are payment, and the price is real. In Christ the substitution is turned around and deepened: the one given is not a foreign people but the Son Himself, who came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. Peter says believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, 1 Peter 1:18-19. The type is outdone in two ways: the price is infinitely higher, and the ransom is paid for people of every nation rather than at their expense.

typology.type: The new thing in the wilderness, verses 19 and 20
typology.fulfillment: Streams in the desert are a picture of the life that God brings where there was none. John records Jesus calling the thirsty to come to Him and drink, John 7:37-38, and tells the Samaritan woman of living water, John 4:10. The correspondence moves from physical water for returning exiles to the Spirit given to all who believe. The wilderness road of Isaiah 40:3 is taken by the Gospels to be the way John prepared for Christ, Mark 1:2-3. The limit is that the returnees found a small, struggling community, Haggai 2:3, and the full renewal only arrives with the new creation, Revelation 21:5.

typology.type: Israel as God's witnesses, verses 10 to 12
typology.fulfillment: Israel was to testify with its life that the LORD alone had foretold and acted. Jesus, before He ascends, tells His disciples, 'You will be My witnesses,' Acts 1:8, using the language of verse 10 in a new setting. The witness now includes the resurrection of Christ, Acts 2:32 and 3:15. The correspondence is that a people of God exists to point to Him. The type is surpassed because the witnesses are now sent to all nations, and because the one to whom they testify has done what no earlier act could, defeating death.

study.christ:
The chapter's central claim is that there is no Savior but the LORD, verse 11, and the New Testament lets that claim stand and then places Jesus within it. Peter says there is salvation in no one else, Acts 4:12, and Paul calls both God the Father and Jesus Christ our Savior in the same letter, Titus 1:3-4 and 2:13. These writers do not treat Jesus as a second savior beside the first. They treat Him as the LORD who saves, which is the same claim that Mark records in the debate over forgiveness, 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?' Mark 2:7. Jesus answers by forgiving, and by healing, to show He has the authority to do so, Mark 2:10-11. The statement of verse 25, 'I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions,' is spoken by God about Himself, and Jesus says it of Himself in the room.

The chapter also speaks of redemption by ransom, verses 1 and 3, and in the Gospels Jesus defines His own mission with that word: He came to give His life as a ransom for many, Mark 10:45. In Isaiah the price is the wealth of nations. The Gospels show that the real price is Himself. Paul can say that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, Galatians 3:13, so the language of a costly purchase in verse 3 reaches its full weight at the cross.

The new exodus comes into view when Luke tells us that Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus on the mountain about His 'departure,' literally His exodus, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem, Luke 9:31. The word links the cross and resurrection with the great rescue of Israel from Egypt, and with the promised return from Babylon, and says that the greater rescue is happening in Him. The 'new thing' is Jesus, and Paul says that if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation, 2 Corinthians 5:17.

The words 'I am He' in verses 10 and 13 are among the passages that help explain why Jesus' use of 'I am' provoked such reaction. When He tells the crowd that they will die in their sins unless they believe that He is, John 8:24, and says before Abraham was born, 'I am,' John 8:58, His hearers pick up stones. They heard Him take the divine self-declaration of Isaiah on His own lips. The chapter does not claim that Jesus is mentioned in these verses; it provides the vocabulary in which the Gospels describe who He is.

The memory-wiping promise of verse 25 comes at the very centre of the new covenant. Jesus says His blood is poured out for the forgiveness of sins, Matthew 26:28, and Hebrews says that the sacrifice of Christ fulfils the promise that God will remember sins no more, Hebrews 10:17-18. The remission of sins 'for My own sake' is thus not a loophole but the way God remains just in forgiving, Romans 3:25-26. A caution: the courtroom of verses 8 to 13 is about the LORD's identity against false gods, and the detail of Israel's witnesses should not be forced into a picture of Christ at every turn.
study.god:
The chapter's God first of all speaks in the first person with unusual force. 'I, yes I' in verses 11 and 25, 'I alone' in verse 12, and 'I am the LORD' in verses 3, 11 and 15 make the whole chapter a self-presentation. He does not describe Himself by comparison with other gods, because there are none to compare. 'Before Me no god was formed, and after Me none will come,' verse 10, claims that He has no ancestry and no successor. He is not a member of a divine family or the winner of a contest among gods.

He is a God who does what He says. The claim in verse 12 is a three-part sequence: He 'decreed, saved and proclaimed.' He announced the rescue before it came, brought it about, and then made it known. This is a God whose word and deed are the same, who can say 'When I act, who can reverse it?' verse 13. The chapter shows power that is not arbitrary, because it is set within a pattern of promise and faithfulness.

He is also a God of astonishing affection. 'You are precious and honored in My sight, and I love you,' verse 4, is one of the plainest statements of love in the prophets. It is spoken to a people who have been blind and deaf. The love is not a reward for their qualities, and the same chapter shows that they have given Him nothing, verses 23 and 24.

God is holy and just, but His justice is not the only thing He is. He can say in verse 24 that Israel has burdened Him and in verse 28 that He will hand them over, and yet in verse 25 declare that He blots out their transgressions for His own sake. The phrase 'for My own sake' shows that He does not forgive because of the sinner's merit or even mainly for the sinner's sake, but because forgiveness expresses who He is. That is not cold; it is the most secure possible ground, because it cannot be lost by anything the sinner does.

The chapter also shows a God who suffers from His people's sin in a way that is startling: 'You have burdened Me with your sins.' Isaiah 63:9 says that in all their distress He too was afflicted. Verse 25's promise to 'remember' no more is not a failure of divine knowledge but a covenant decision not to hold sins against them.

For worship, the chapter calls for an answer to its charge in verse 22: that the people have not called on Him. The right response is to call, confident that He who created, formed, redeemed and named them is also the one who forgives for His own sake.

crossReferences.note: The sea parted and Israel crossed on dry ground between walls of water. Isaiah 43:2 and 43:16 take this picture and turn it into a promise for the future, so the exiles are told that the God of the sea crossing is the God of their return.

The psalmist says that the people went through fire and water and were then brought to a place of abundance. It reads like a summary of Isaiah 43:2 as already experienced, and shows that the promise of verse 2 belongs to the worship of Israel as well as to prophecy.

The LORD says that He has been Israel's God since Egypt, and that there is no Savior besides Him. This is the older form of Isaiah 43:11, which means that the prophet is not inventing a new claim but restating the oldest line of Israel's faith.

A cry to the arm of the LORD to wake up as it did in the days of old, when it dried up the sea and made a road for the redeemed to cross. It is a prayer built on Isaiah 43:16-19, asking God to act again in the pattern of the exodus.

Jesus says the Son of Man came to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many. The ransom of Isaiah 43:3 is a costly exchange, and Jesus shows what is exchanged: not foreign nations but His own life, so that the many are freed.

Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about His departure, literally His exodus, that He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. The word links Jesus' death and resurrection directly with the new exodus promised in Isaiah 43:16-19.

Peter stands before the rulers and says salvation is found in no one else, and that no other name under heaven has been given among men by which we must be saved. It is Isaiah 43:11 in the mouth of an apostle, with Jesus as the name.

Jesus says that before Abraham was born, 'I am,' and His hearers try to stone Him. His words draw on the self-declaration of God in Isaiah, such as the 'I am He' of 43:10 and 43:13, and they understood that He was claiming what belongs to God alone.

Jesus tells His disciples they will be His witnesses to the ends of the earth. The commission re-uses the role Isaiah 43:10 gives to Israel, 'You are My witnesses,' and widens it from a nation in a courtroom to a worldwide company testifying to the risen Lord.

The writer quotes the promise to remember sins no more and draws the conclusion that where these are forgiven there is no more offering for sin. It takes Isaiah 43:25 and its echo in Jeremiah 31:34 as fulfilled in the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ.

Paul says that anyone in Christ is a new creation, that the old has passed and the new has come. It gathers the 'new thing' of Isaiah 43:19 and the creation language of verse 1 and says that they are real now for those who belong to Christ.

study.oneStory:
Isaiah 43 begins with creation and ends in forgiveness, and the whole Bible is arranged on that line. The opening words, 'He who created you,' send the reader back to Genesis, where God made a people to bear His image and live in His presence. Everything that follows in the chapter, the fear, the scattering and the weariness, is what happens to the creation after Genesis 3. The chapter's answer is not to abandon the creation, but to redeem it, and the word redeem points back to the exodus, the great act in which God first claimed Israel as His own.

The chapter then holds two stories together. The first is rescue: God buys back, gathers and brings home. The second is accusation: Israel did not call on Him, and its first father sinned, verse 27. The reader sees the full plot of Scripture compressed into a single page, with a God who rescues and a people who keep falling, and the tension is resolved only in verse 25, where God says that He Himself will deal with the sin. That is the promise that the rest of the Old Testament waits for.

The new exodus sets the pattern for how later writers speak of salvation. The return from Babylon is the first step, though a modest one. The prophets look to a greater rescue, which the New Testament says was accomplished in Christ's departure at Jerusalem, Luke 9:31, and which the church now lives in as a company of witnesses gathered from every direction, John 11:52 and Acts 1:8.

The story ends where Isaiah 43:19 points. The God who makes a way in the wilderness will make all things new, and the one who says 'I am doing something new' in Isaiah says it again from the throne in the final chapters of Scripture, Revelation 21:5. The sins that He has blotted out will not be remembered, Revelation 21:4 says that the former things have passed away, and those who were created for His glory, verse 7, will finally live in it.

quiz.q: What promise does the LORD give in verses 1 to 2 regarding waters and fire?

options.text: When Israel passes through waters or fire, the LORD will be with them and they will not be overwhelmed or scorched.
options.note: Verses 1 to 2 state this promise of presence and protection directly.

options.text: Israel will never face any hardship or trial again.
options.note: The promise is God's presence through trials, not the total absence of trials.

options.text: Only the wealthy among Israel will be protected.
options.note: The promise is given to the whole people, called by name, not a wealthy subset.

options.text: Israel must earn this protection through additional sacrifices.
options.note: The promise flows from being redeemed and called by name, not from additional required sacrifices.

quiz.q: What exclusive claim does the LORD make in verse 11?

options.text: There is no Savior but Me.
options.note: Verse 11 states this exclusive claim directly, echoed in Acts 4:12 regarding Christ.

options.text: Other nations have equally valid saviors.
options.note: The opposite; the LORD claims to be the only Savior, with no rivals.

options.text: Salvation is available through many different gods.
options.note: The verse insists on exclusivity, not a plurality of valid saviors.

options.text: Salvation will come only through human effort.
options.note: The claim is that the LORD alone saves, not that salvation depends on human effort.

quiz.q: What does the LORD announce He is about to do in verses 18 to 19?

options.text: A new thing, making a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert.
options.note: Verse 19 announces exactly this new thing, echoing the exodus pattern.

options.text: A return to exactly the former things, with nothing new.
options.note: The opposite; the LORD explicitly says not to dwell on the former things, since He is doing something new.

options.text: The permanent destruction of Israel with no restoration.
options.note: The announcement is one of hope and provision, not destruction.

options.text: A command to remain in exile permanently.
options.note: The announcement describes a way of deliverance and provision, not permanent exile.

quiz.q: What honest diagnosis does the LORD give of Israel in verses 22 to 24?

options.text: They grew weary of Him, did not call on Him, and burdened Him with their sins rather than honoring Him with sacrifices.
options.note: These verses state this diagnosis directly and honestly.

options.text: Israel had perfectly fulfilled every requirement of worship.
options.note: The opposite; the passage describes failure and neglect in worship, not perfect fulfillment.

options.text: Israel over-sacrificed to the point of exhausting the priests.
options.note: The text says the opposite: Israel did not bring sacrifices or honor God with offerings.

options.text: The failure described belongs only to a few individuals, not the nation.
options.note: The diagnosis is addressed to Jacob and Israel collectively, describing a national pattern, not isolated individuals.

quiz.q: On what basis does the LORD blot out Israel's transgressions in verse 25?

options.text: For His own sake, not because Israel earned or deserved it.
options.note: Verse 25 states this directly: 'for My own sake,' grounding forgiveness in God's character, not merit.

options.text: Because Israel offered sufficient sacrifices to earn forgiveness.
options.note: The preceding verses explicitly say Israel had not honored God with sacrifices; forgiveness is not earned here.

options.text: Because Israel's ancestors had lived faultlessly.
options.note: The following verses actually recall the sin of Israel's 'first father' and spokesmen, not faultless ancestry.

options.text: Because Babylon requested it on Israel's behalf.
options.note: The forgiveness is entirely between the LORD and Israel, grounded in God's own character, not a third party's request.

questions: The LORD promises His presence through waters and fire, not the absence of trials. What waters or fire are you currently walking through, and how does knowing God is with you in it change your posture?
The LORD declares there is no Savior but Him, a claim the New Testament applies fully to Jesus. Where are you tempted to look for salvation, security, or rescue outside of Christ?
God announces a new thing and asks, 'do you not see it?' What might God be doing that is new in your life right now that you have not yet noticed or acknowledged?
Israel's failure was not dramatic rebellion but simply growing weary of God and no longer calling on Him. Has your own relationship with God grown into quiet neglect rather than active dependence?
God blots out transgressions for His own sake, not because they are earned. How does resting in grace rather than performance change the way you approach your own failures this week?

translationNotes.note: Egypt, Cush, and Seba given 'in your place' most likely reflects the historical pattern of Cyrus receiving these regions in exchange for releasing the Jewish exiles, though the text frames it as God's own sovereign exchange for His people's sake.
The Hebrew idiom behind 'even now it is coming' emphasizes the nearness and certainty of this promised new deliverance, not a distant or merely hoped-for future event.
Your first father most likely refers to Jacob, or possibly Adam, as the archetypal ancestor whose sin set the pattern the nation's spokesmen, its later leaders, continued to repeat.
